extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers and practitioners studying LLM capabilities and AGI
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the capabilities, limitations, and societal implications of large language models (GPT-4) via experiments across multiple domains (language, vision, coding, math, tool use, human interaction) and comparison to prior models and human performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of AGI (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: AGI: systems that demonstrate broad capabilities of intelligence, including reasoning, planning, and the ability to learn from experience, and with these capabilities at or above human-level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative benchmark for whether a system is progressing toward AGI; the paper notes alternate definitions exist and discusses them in conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of natural language
rubrics_metrics.description: Can generate fluent and coherent text, translate between natural languages, change tone and style, and translate across domains (medicine, law, programming, music, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes fluency/coherence and ability to manipulate complex concepts; evaluated via varied prompts and style/genre shifts (e.g., poetic proof, Plato dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality / Integrative ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to understand and connect topics across modalities and disciplines, performing tasks that go beyond narrow, well-defined tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by providing tasks from many domains and checking whether the model can combine skills (e.g., generate code that produces visual output, combine math reasoning and poetic form). Emphasized as central to claims of progress toward AGI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard benchmark evaluation (independence from training data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the system on standard benchmark datasets, ensuring they are independent of the training data and cover a range of tasks and domains to separate true learning from memorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper cautions that for GPT-4 exact training data are unknown, so benchmarks may have been seen by the model; thus benchmark results should be interpreted carefully and supplemented by other probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruling out memorization (novelty of tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design novel and difficult tasks and vary prompts to ensure outputs are not mere memorization or copying from training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: modify code (remove horn), change prompts/styles, remove textual hints; probe robustness by asking for variations and improvements to generated artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation on generative/interactive tasks (beyond single-solution benchmarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess performance on tasks that do not admit a single solution (e.g., GUI creation, brainstorming, generative design), recognizing that metrics are challenging to define.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper suggests psychology-style human creativity probes alongside benchmarks; acknowledges need for new evaluation methods since automatic scoring is difficult for such tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding ability and practical engineer metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to follow instructions to produce code, understand and modify existing code, and perform in coding interviews (LeetCode) with metrics such as time, testcases solved, and LeetCode scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper reports LeetCode Interview Assessment results (scores and percentiles) and highlights speed (solves rounds in allotted time); suggests coding performance as emblematic of reasoning capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical reasoning and modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Capability to carry out mathematical conversations, solve problems from math datasets, perform mathematical modeling across domains, and engage in higher-level mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes probing via interactive conversation variants, checking for calculation errors, generalization, and use of external code execution to mitigate arithmetic mistakes (Appendix D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision & multimodal abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Image generation beyond memorization, following detailed image instructions, sketch generation and other vision-enabled tasks; also ability to 'comprehend' code/graphics that represent images (e.g., TikZ unicorn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper emphasizes multimodal composition and integrative tasks; notes the tested version was text-only but demonstrates capability to reason about visual code and to update drawings based on edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool use and interaction with the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to use multiple tools to solve complex tasks and to interact with environments (text-based games, simulated environments), including chaining tools and composing actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes experiments on tool use, multi-tool pipelines, and text-based/embodied interaction warmups; assesses whether tool usage expands effective capabilities and planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied interaction and planning in environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance in embodied or simulated settings (navigating maps, text-based games) to evaluate planning, sequential decision-making, and learning within episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper examines warmups, text-game play, and real-world problem simulations to reveal planning strengths and weaknesses (Section 5.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Mind / understanding humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to infer human motives, beliefs, and emotions (theory of mind), tested via specific tasks and realistic scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes targeted tests of aspects of theory of mind and discussion of results and limitations (Section 6.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability / communicating to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to explain reasoning and outputs in ways humans can understand; produce explanations that clarify decisions and internal reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed by evaluating how well the model makes itself understandable and provides explanations (Section 6.2); relates to human trust and usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminative capabilities (PII detection, fact-checking, misconceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to detect Personally Identifiable Information (PII), correct misconceptions, and perform fact-checking and discrimination among candidate answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper highlights limitations of current metrics for these tasks, experiments where GPT-4 acts as a judge, and detailed category breakdowns of performance (Section 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations due to autoregressive architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific failure modes attributed to autoregressive next-token prediction: lack of planning in arithmetic/reasoning problems and in text generation; potential need to move beyond next-word prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 8 gives warm-up examples and in-depth analysis; used to motivate future paradigms and to interpret what emergent behaviors may lack (e.g., extended planning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of human-level performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare model outputs to human performance on benchmarks and tests (e.g., USMLE Step exams, Multistate Bar, LeetCode) and judge whether model is at or beyond human-level in given domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper reports approximate accuracies (~80% on USMLE components, ~70% on Multistate Bar) and LeetCode scores with percentiles; stresses these are preliminary estimates and may change with model evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology: psychology-style probing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use human creativity to design novel probes, vary prompts, probe for consistency/coherence/correctness, and emphasize discovering limitations and biases rather than relying solely on formal benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors acknowledge subjectivity of this approach but argue it's necessary to explore generality; combine with benchmarks and ablations for a fuller picture (Section 1.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats about versions, training dynamics, and interpretability of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative results are estimates for an early development version; the model changed over time so results may differ on final deployed versions; interpreted results should account for training evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated throughout paper: treat numbers as estimates of potential; the tested system was text-only for inputs; improvements occurred during the testing window (Figure 1.3 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning vs. non-continuous updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between within-session (fast) learning and slow training-time improvements; the tested GPT-4 does not continuously update across sessions, though it can learn within a session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important when assessing claims about 'learning from experience' as an AGI trait; the system's inability to perform continuous online learning is a limitation to be considered (Section 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal impact and safety considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess challenges caused by erroneous generations (hallucinations), misinformation and manipulation, bias, and impacts on human expertise, jobs, and economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper devotes Section 9 to these issues, arguing that capability advances bring both benefits and risks and must be discussed alongside technical evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of current metrics and use of model-as-judge pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Current automatic or proxy metrics can be insufficient (especially for misconceptions/fact-checking and generative tasks); using models to judge outputs (e.g., 'Judge GPT-4') risks bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper documents examples where GPT-4 prefers its own outputs and discusses why new benchmarks and human-in-the-loop evaluation are needed (Section 7.2).
